title: Union & Intersection Types
summary: A **union** (`A | B`) means a value is *one of* several types; an **intersection** (`A & B`) means a value has *all of* several types at once. Unions model alternatives and require narrowing to use safely; intersections combine shapes into a richer one.

subtopics.title: Union types (A | B)
subtopics.explanation: A union type means a value can be any one of the listed types. string | number accepts a string or a number. You can only use members that are common to every member of the union until you narrow it, because TypeScript doesn't know which one you currently have.

subtopics.title: Intersection types (A & B)
subtopics.explanation: An intersection combines multiple types into one that has all their members simultaneously. A & B has every property of A and of B. It's most useful for merging object shapes — the result must satisfy every part at the same time.

subtopics.title: Narrowing a union
subtopics.explanation: To use a union safely you narrow it — use a runtime check that tells the compiler which member you have. typeof, instanceof, 'in', or comparing to a literal all narrow. Inside the checked branch, TypeScript treats the value as the specific member.

subtopics.title: Unions of literals
subtopics.explanation: Unions are most powerful with literal types: 'sm' | 'md' | 'lg' is a closed set of allowed values, far safer than string. The compiler rejects any value outside the set and gives autocomplete for the valid ones.

subtopics.title: Combining object types with &
subtopics.explanation: Intersections build bigger object types from smaller ones, an alternative to interface extends. Props & { onClose: () => void } adds a property to an existing shape. The combined type requires every property from each operand.
subtopics.example:
type Base = { id: number };
type Timestamped = Base & { createdAt: number };

subtopics.title: When to use each
subtopics.explanation: Use a union when a value is one of several alternatives (a status that is 'loading' or 'error'). Use an intersection when a value must satisfy several shapes at once (an entity that is both identifiable and named). Union = OR, intersection = AND.
subtopics.example:
type Result = Success | Failure; // OR
type FullUser = User & Audit; // AND

subtopics.title: Exhaustiveness checking
subtopics.explanation: When you switch over a union, you can guarantee every case is handled by assigning the leftover value to a never-typed variable in the default branch. If a new union member is added later, this assignment fails to compile, forcing you to handle it.
subtopics.example: const _exhaustive: never = value; // errors if a case is missed

foundations.overview: Union and intersection types are TypeScript's two ways of composing types. Unions express 'one of' (alternatives) and are the basis of modeling states, options, and varying inputs; intersections express 'all of' (combination) and merge shapes. Together they let you describe real-world data precisely.
foundations.formalDefinition: A union type A | B is the set of values assignable to A or to B. An intersection type A & B is the set of values assignable to both A and B simultaneously. Members of a union expose only their common API until narrowed.
foundations.whyItMatters: Unions (especially of literals) are how idiomatic TypeScript models finite states and options safely, and narrowing is a core skill. Interviewers test unions, narrowing, and exhaustiveness to gauge whether you can model data without resorting to any.
foundations.mentalModel: Picture sets of values. A union is the combined region of two sets (OR) — a value lands in either. An intersection is the overlap (AND) — a value must lie in both, so it carries every property of each.
foundations.browserPerspective: Both are compile-time only and erased at emit. The narrowing checks you write (typeof, in, instanceof) are real JavaScript that runs in the browser, but the union/intersection types themselves leave no runtime trace.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Component props that accept variants, API responses that are success-or-error, configuration options as literal unions, and merging base + extension shapes via intersection are all everyday uses.
foundations.businessImpact: Modeling states and options as unions prevents whole classes of invalid-state bugs from shipping, improving reliability of user-facing features.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Unions plus exhaustiveness checks make adding a new state a compile-guided task — the compiler points to every place that must handle it, reducing missed cases.
foundations.performanceImpact: No runtime cost from the types themselves. Very large unions can slow type-checking and editor responsiveness, so keep unions reasonably sized.
commonUseCases: Modeling finite states with literal unions ('loading' | 'success' | 'error')
Accepting flexible inputs like string | number
Combining object shapes with intersections (Base & Extension)
Discriminated unions for API responses and reducer actions

commonMisconceptions.myth: A | B lets you use any member of either type immediately.
commonMisconceptions.reality: You can only use the common members until you narrow; otherwise the compiler can't be sure which type you have.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Intersections of conflicting primitives just pick one.
commonMisconceptions.reality: string & number has no possible value — it reduces to never — because nothing can be both at once.

config.intro: Follow a value typed string | number through a typeof check.

steps.name: Declare the union
steps.detail: let id: string | number means id is one of the two, but not known which at compile time.

steps.name: Restricted usage
steps.detail: Before narrowing, only members common to string and number are allowed — string-specific methods are rejected.

steps.name: Add a narrowing check
steps.detail: if (typeof id === 'string') is real runtime code the compiler understands as a type guard.

steps.name: Narrow in the branch
steps.detail: Inside the if, TypeScript narrows id to string, so string methods become available and checked.

steps.name: The else branch
steps.detail: In the else, id is narrowed to number — each branch sees the precise member, never the whole union.

interactiveExamples.title: A union with narrowing
interactiveExamples.explanation: The same parameter handles a string or number; a typeof check narrows it so each branch uses the right operations.

interactiveExamples.title: Intersection combines two object shapes
interactiveExamples.explanation: An intersection requires every property of both shapes; the value must satisfy all of them at once.

codeLab.title: Narrow a union to print the right output
codeLab.instructions: describe takes a boolean | string. Add a narrowing check so booleans print 'yes'/'no' and strings print their length. The starter doesn't narrow yet.
hints: Use typeof value === 'boolean' to narrow to the boolean branch.
In the remaining branch value is narrowed to string, so value.length is available.

debuggingLab.title: Using a union member without narrowing
debuggingLab.symptom: Code calls a string-only method on a string | number value, which TypeScript rejects (and would crash if forced through with any).
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Without narrowing, toUpperCase isn't valid on the whole union. The code silences the error with 'as any', so the number path reaches a method that doesn't exist and throws at runtime.
commonMistakes: Casting a union to any to suppress the error instead of narrowing.
Assuming a string-only method is safe on the entire union.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Narrow the union with typeof and handle the number case explicitly instead of casting.

theory.question: What is the difference between a union (A | B) and an intersection (A & B)?
theory.directAnswer: A union means a value is one of the listed types (OR) — string | number is a string or a number, and you can only use common members until you narrow. An intersection means a value is all of the listed types at once (AND) — A & B has every property of both, useful for merging object shapes.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two type composition operators: | for alternatives and & for combination.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Real values are sometimes 'one of several' (union) and sometimes 'a combination of several' (intersection); TypeScript needs both to model them.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: A union is the set of values in either type; an intersection is the set in both. Unions expose only common members until narrowed; intersections expose all members.

theory.whyImportant: Choosing union vs intersection correctly is fundamental to modeling data, and unions underpin discriminated unions and state modeling.
theory.realWorldExample: A status is 'idle' | 'loading' | 'done' (union); a logged-in user might be User & { token: string } (intersection).

nestedTopics.title: Common members
nestedTopics.explanation: Only members shared by all union arms are usable before narrowing.

nestedTopics.title: Merging shapes
nestedTopics.explanation: Intersections combine object types similarly to interface extends.

nestedTopics.title: never from conflicts
nestedTopics.explanation: An intersection of incompatible primitives like string & number is never.

followUps.question: Why can't you call a string method on a string | number directly?
followUps.answer: TypeScript only allows members common to every arm; toUpperCase isn't on number, so you must narrow to string first.

followUps.question: What does string & number evaluate to?
followUps.answer: never — no value can be both a string and a number simultaneously.

theory.question: What is narrowing and how do you narrow a union type?
theory.directAnswer: Narrowing is reducing a value's type to a more specific one based on a runtime check the compiler understands. For unions you narrow with typeof (for primitives), instanceof (for classes), the 'in' operator (for property presence), or comparing a discriminant property to a literal. Inside the checked branch the value is treated as the specific member.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The process of moving from a broad union type to a precise member within a control-flow branch.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Because you can't safely use member-specific operations on a whole union — you must first establish which member you have.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: TypeScript's control-flow analysis tracks guards like typeof x === 'string' and refines the type within the branch they guard.

theory.whyImportant: Narrowing is the everyday skill that makes unions usable; without it, unions force you toward unsafe casts.
theory.realWorldExample: Handling a string | number id by typeof-checking before formatting it differently in each branch.

nestedTopics.title: typeof guards
nestedTopics.explanation: Narrow primitives by their typeof string.

nestedTopics.title: in / instanceof
nestedTopics.explanation: Narrow object unions by property presence or constructor.

nestedTopics.title: Discriminant narrowing
nestedTopics.explanation: Compare a shared literal field (e.g. kind) to pick an arm.

followUps.question: What's a discriminated union?
followUps.answer: A union of object types sharing a literal 'tag' field (like kind), letting you narrow by switching on that field — the cleanest pattern for variant data.

scenario.question: Your API client returns either a success payload or an error object, and the calling code keeps forgetting to handle the error case. How would you model and enforce this with types?
scenario.directAnswer: Model the result as a discriminated union: type Result = { status: 'ok'; data: User } | { status: 'error'; message: string }. Callers switch on status, and you add an exhaustiveness check (assigning the default case to a never variable) so that if a new variant is added, every consumer that doesn't handle it fails to compile.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Using a literal-discriminated union plus exhaustiveness checking to force handling of every case.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: An untyped 'maybe success, maybe error' shape lets callers ignore the error path; a discriminated union makes the alternatives explicit.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Switching on the discriminant narrows each branch; the never assignment in default errors if any member is unhandled.

scenario.whyImportant: Modeling success/error as a union is the canonical way TypeScript prevents unhandled-state bugs at compile time.

nestedTopics.title: Discriminant field
nestedTopics.explanation: A shared literal property (status) that distinguishes the arms.

nestedTopics.title: Exhaustiveness
nestedTopics.explanation: A never assignment guarantees the compiler flags missed cases.

followUps.question: Why not use intersection here instead?
followUps.answer: The value is one of two shapes, not both at once — that's OR, so a union is correct; an intersection would require it to be success and error simultaneously.

coding.question: Write a function area that takes a shape union (circle or square) and returns its area, using a discriminated union and an exhaustiveness check.
coding.thoughtProcess: I model the input as a discriminated union with a 'kind' tag: { kind: 'circle'; radius } | { kind: 'square'; side }. I switch on kind so each branch is narrowed to the right shape. In the default I assign the value to a never variable so adding a new shape later forces me to handle it.
coding.lineByLine: Shape is a union of two object types sharing the literal field kind. Switching on shape.kind narrows each case to the matching shape, so radius/side are only accessible where valid. The default assigns shape to a never variable — if a third kind is added, that assignment fails to compile, enforcing exhaustiveness.
coding.timeComplexity: O(1) — a fixed branch and arithmetic.

alternativeApproaches.title: if/else on kind
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Works the same but the never-based exhaustiveness check is harder to wire up cleanly than in a switch default.

followUps.question: How does the never assignment enforce exhaustiveness?
followUps.answer: If every case is handled, shape is narrowed to never in default and the assignment compiles; an unhandled member leaves a non-never type, which isn't assignable to never, producing a compile error.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Unions (especially discriminated unions) model variant data across a system — reducer actions, API results, UI states — while intersections compose shared shapes into richer ones. Centralizing these in shared types keeps variants consistent.
productionDeepDive.performance: Types are erased, so there's no runtime cost beyond the narrowing checks you write. Very large unions can slow the type-checker and editor; keep them bounded and prefer discriminated unions for clarity.
productionDeepDive.security: Type-level unions don't validate runtime data — an API that claims to return a union still needs runtime validation, because a malformed response could violate the assumed shape.
productionDeepDive.scaling: Discriminated unions plus exhaustiveness checks make adding a new variant a compiler-guided change: the build points to every site that must handle it, which scales safely across many consumers.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Prefer unions over loose optional flags for variant data, and intersections over duplicating shared fields. Exhaustiveness checks keep switches honest as variants evolve.
productionDeepDive.observability: tsc --noEmit in CI catches missing union cases via exhaustiveness checks and rejects unnarrowed usage, surfacing modeling gaps before runtime.

caseStudies.problem: Action and response variants were modeled loosely, so new variants silently went unhandled.
caseStudies.solution: Discriminated unions with a 'type'/'status' tag and never-based exhaustiveness checks in switches.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Slightly more upfront type structure for guaranteed case coverage.
caseStudies.lessons: Unions plus exhaustiveness turn 'forgot a case' bugs into compile errors.

steps.checkpoint: Each status carries only its relevant fields.

keyTakeaways: A union (A | B) means a value is one of several types; an intersection (A & B) means it has all of them at once.
You can only use members common to a union until you narrow it with typeof, instanceof, 'in', or a literal check.
Intersections merge object shapes; conflicting primitive intersections collapse to never.
Use unions for alternatives (OR) and intersections for combination (AND).
Discriminated unions plus a never-based default give compile-time exhaustiveness so missed cases become errors.
